opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing about Kaiming He is his taste: his sense of which problems are worth working on, and what form a good solution should take. When you look at his body of work, ResNet, Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN, MoCo, MAE, you notice that almost none of these papers are complicated. ResNet is essentially adding an identity shortcut. MAE is essentially masking a large portion of image patches and reconstructing them. You could explain the core idea in one sentence. But that simplicity is not luck. It comes from a very deep understanding of where the real bottleneck is.

With ResNet, for example, many people at the time thought deeper networks were hard to train because of vanishing gradients, and the usual response was to add more tricks. Kaiming looked at it differently. He observed that even the training error got worse as you went deeper, which shouldn't happen if a deeper network can at least copy a shallower one. So the question became: why can't the network easily learn an identity mapping? Once you frame the problem that way, the residual connection is almost the natural answer. I think that is his strength: he spends a lot of effort finding the right framing, and then the solution becomes simple.

The second thing is his extremely high standard for experiments. His papers are known for being very solid. The ablations are thorough, the baselines are fair, and the claims are carefully scoped. People trust his results, and they can reproduce them. That builds a kind of credibility that compounds over time. When a paper from him comes out, the community takes it seriously because they know it will work.

Third, he is patient and focused. He doesn't publish a huge number of papers, and he doesn't chase every trend. He will stay on one important direction, like visual representation learning, for years, and keep asking the fundamental questions. Many people in AI today feel pressure to publish fast and follow whatever is hot. Kaiming is a good counterexample. Fewer but more fundamental works can have far more impact.

Finally, I think he really values generality. His methods tend to become infrastructure: residual connections are now in basically every large model, including Transformers. He isn't optimizing for a benchmark number. He's looking for something that other people can build on. In the long run, that is what defines great research: not how clever the method looks, but how many people end up using it without even thinking about it.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: That's a question a lot of people in our field have thought about, because Kaiming is almost a singular case. ResNet, Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN, MoCo, MAE—each one of those would be a career-defining paper for most researchers, and he has done it repeatedly, across different eras of the field.

If I try to explain it, I'd point to a few things.

The first is taste. He has an extraordinary sense for which problems actually matter and which ones are just fashionable. He doesn't chase whatever is hot that month. He asks: what is the fundamental bottleneck right now? With ResNet, the whole community knew deeper networks should be better but couldn't train them. He didn't invent some exotic new architecture—he found the simplest possible fix, the identity shortcut, and that one idea unlocked everything.

That leads to the second thing, which is his pursuit of simplicity. If you read his papers, they're remarkably clean. Very few moving parts, very few tricks. MAE is a good example—mask most of the image, reconstruct the pixels, done. People had tried similar things before and it didn't work well. His contribution was to strip away the unnecessary assumptions and find the version that actually works. Simple methods are the ones that survive and get built on, and I think he understands that deeply.

The third is rigor in experiments. He is extremely careful about ablations and about making sure a result is real and not an artifact of some hyperparameter. When a Kaiming paper says something works, people trust it, and that trust compounds over a career.

And I'd add one more, which is less visible from the outside: patience and focus. He doesn't publish a huge volume of papers. He spends a long time on each problem, iterates quietly, and only releases when the idea is really crystallized. In an environment where everyone feels pressure to put out something every conference cycle, that discipline is rare.

So I wouldn't say there's a secret. It's taste in picking problems, a relentless drive toward simplicity, careful experimentation, and the patience to do fewer things very well. Any one of those is learnable. Having all of them together, consistently, for fifteen years—that's what makes him exceptional.

astra-6.text:
I’d point to his ability to identify a fundamental problem and then find a remarkably clear way to address it. Take residual learning: as networks get deeper, making them train effectively becomes a central challenge. The idea of learning a residual gives you a simple way to rethink that challenge, with enormous practical consequences.

But the simplicity of the final idea can be misleading. Getting there requires strong intuition, careful experiments, and a willingness to keep questioning why something works. I think that combination—choosing important problems and investigating them deeply—is a big part of his success. Of course, that’s my reading of his research, rather than a claim about how he personally approaches every project.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about attributing his success to a single trait. My impression is that he has an exceptional ability to identify a fundamental problem and find a simple, effective way to address it. That sounds straightforward, but deciding which problem matters—and stripping away unnecessary complexity—is very difficult.

There’s also the rigor of the work: having an elegant idea is one thing; testing it carefully and understanding why it works is another. I think that combination of problem selection, clarity, and persistent experimentation helps explain his success. Of course, that’s my interpretation, rather than something I can claim to know about his personal process.
